title: POC scoping - Integration planning with Nimbus Health
summary: AE + SE from Redwood scoped a 6-week POC to validate integration with Nimbus Health's care-coordination product. Primary goals: 1) validate OpenAI-compatible SDK integration and structured output/function calling; 2) run latency and cost benchmarks at expected 8-12 RPS and p95 latency <200ms for short chat flows; 3) confirm security/compliance fit for PHI (SOC2, KMS, VPC). Agreed next steps: Redwood to run a benchmark using Nimbus sample prompts, provide security pack and pricing for hosted vs dedicated, and schedule a 2-week pilot kickoff.
next_steps: Redwood: run benchmark with Nimbus sample dataset and report p50/p95 latencies and cost estimates (due 2025-04-09)
Redwood: send security & compliance pack (SOC 2, ISO, SAML/KMS notes) and reference deployment docs (due 2025-04-04)
Nimbus: share a sanitized sample of 500 prompts + expected system messages and desired JSON schema for structured output (due 2025-04-04)
Schedule pilot kickoff meeting (2-week pilot) — propose 2025-04-14 for kickoff
action_items: Sophie Chen: Send security/compliance pack and Redwood POC checklist — due 2025-04-04
Ethan Park: Run benchmark (hosted and dedicated config) against provided sample set and share results + runbook — due 2025-04-09
Priya Natarajan: Share sanitized sample prompts + expected output schema and example function definitions — due 2025-04-04
Daniel Reyes: Confirm internal stakeholders for pilot and procurement timeline — due 2025-04-07
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-02
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 58 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Sophie Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Daniel Reyes (Nimbus CTO), Priya Natarajan (Nimbus ML Eng), Alex Martinez (Nimbus PM)

00:00 Sophie Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick note, this is being recorded by Fireflies, we will share transcript and notes. Uh, why don't we do quick intros — Ethan, do you want to kick off?
00:12 Ethan Park: Yeah, sure. Ethan Park, Redwood systems engineering — I focus on integration and benchmark runs, happy to dig into throughput and latency stuff.
00:18 Daniel Reyes: Daniel, CTO at Nimbus — we're primarily focused on care coordination workflows, some PHI, looking to add assistant features in the product.
00:25 Priya Natarajan: Priya, ML engineer, I'll own the POC on the Nimbus side. We'll provide sample prompts and the evaluation set.
00:32 Alex Martinez: Alex, product — I'll be tracking success metrics and timeline.
00:35 Sophie Chen: Great. High level purpose today: scope a POC — integration plan, success criteria, workload sizing, benchmarks, and timelines. We'll also cover security/deployment questions.
00:45 Daniel Reyes: To start, our main success criteria — one, we need structured JSON output for our downstream system (we'll send schema); two, latency has to be reasonable — targeting p95 under 200ms for short interactions, and three, cost needs to be predictable. We also need to make sure PHI is handled per our compliance.
01:05 Ethan Park: Good. A couple clarifying Qs: when you say short interactions, is that like 1-2 user messages plus a short assistant reply, or longer documents?
01:12 Alex Martinez: Mostly short chat flows — triage questions, suggested care instructions. Average prompt size is around 350–500 tokens; expected completion usually 80–150 tokens.
01:22 Priya Natarajan: Concurrency-wise we expect peak 8–12 requests per second during clinic hours, with spikes maybe up to 20 for brief periods. Monthly active users estimate leads to roughly 100M tokens/month in the POC projection.
01:36 Sophie Chen: That helps a lot. For the POC we typically run a 2-week pilot that proves integration and correctness, then a 4-week scale validation for performance/cost — total ~6 weeks. Does that work for you?
01:48 Daniel Reyes: That timeline seems fine as long as we can show the p95 numbers in the scale validation.
01:55 Ethan Park: Implementation plan: we support OpenAI-compatible endpoints — you can swap in by changing base URL and key. We also have SDKs for Node/Python that mirror OpenAI surface area, plus direct REST examples. Function-calling and structured output are supported; we can do enforced JSON schema or function-like calls to ensure well-formed output.
02:12 Priya Natarajan: Are the function calls exactly like OpenAI's format or are there differences? We use generated functions to trigger actions downstream.
02:18 Ethan Park: We mimic the same semantics: function name, args as JSON, etc. There are some Redwood-specific optimizations around streaming and partial outputs, but the developer experience is the same. If you want guaranteed schema, we can use the structured-output feature and run an auto-parser to validate.
02:30 Alex Martinez: For our product, we want two things: 1) a deterministic JSON with keys the downstream system expects; 2) function invocations for calls like "create-referral" with arguments.
02:40 Sophie Chen: We can do both. For the POC we'll validate the JSON schema on Redwood's side and show how function calls map to webhook/queue events in your system.
02:50 Daniel Reyes: Security questions: can you run in a VPC? How is KMS handled? We need to know about audit logs and SOC2.
02:58 Sophie Chen: Yes — Redwood Private supports VPC and customer-managed networking. For hosted we offer private networking options for enterprise. Keys can be customer-managed with KMS/HSM integrations; we also provide audit logs and retention controls. We'll send the SOC2 and ISO docs in the security pack.
03:15 Priya Natarajan: What about data retention and purging? For PHI we need logs purged after X days and strict access control.
03:22 Sophie Chen: We can configure retention policies and redact logs. We'll include retention settings in the docs; for the POC we can set a short window and limit access.
03:30 Ethan Park: On benchmarks — to set expectations, with 350–500 token prompts and 80–150 token completions, and the concurrency numbers you gave, we can run an A/B: Redwood hosted API vs Redwood Dedicated (reserved capacity) vs an open-source baseline (self-hosted) to measure p50/p95 latency and cost per 1k tokens. We'll provide a spreadsheet with assumptions.
03:48 Priya Natarajan: For the open-source baseline, we care about quantized performance. We may already have a small infra experiment, but we want to see how Redwood's runtime performs.
03:56 Ethan Park: Understood. We'll include quantization profiles in the recommendations and show the tradeoffs (cost vs latency vs quality). We'll also report per-token cost estimates for your workload and expected autoscaling behavior.
04:08 Alex Martinez: How do we handle streaming? Some interactions rely on partial updates to the UI.
04:12 Ethan Park: Streaming is supported in the same way as OpenAI (chunked events). We expose SSE/websocket patterns. There are a few differences in chunk sizes to optimize latency, we'll document them.
04:22 Daniel Reyes: For metrics and observability — we need tracing into our app and token-level costing.
04:28 Sophie Chen: Redwood Console gives per-route and per-token breakdowns, tracing hooks, and you can push traces down into your observability stack. We'll include a sample dashboard export and tracing integration notes.
04:40 Priya Natarajan: For the POC success criteria, can we define pass/fail? It helps us decide whether to proceed to Dedicated.
04:47 Sophie Chen: Sure — proposed success criteria for POC: (1) Integration: SDK+endpoint integration completed and structured output validated on 95% of test cases; (2) Latency: p95 under 200ms for simulated short flows at target concurrency during scale validation; (3) Cost: cost projection within 15% of the spreadsheet estimate; (4) Security: SOC2 + KMS and retention requirements satisfied and documentation reviewed.
05:09 Daniel Reyes: That seems good. One more question: how do webhooks/function calls look in failures? We need reliable retry semantics.
05:16 Ethan Park: Webhooks for function invocations are retried with exponential backoff and we persist events to a queue you control if needed. For POC we'll set up a test endpoint to exercise error paths.
05:26 Alex Martinez: On the procurement side, if we move to Dedicated, what's the lead time?
05:30 Sophie Chen: Typical lead time for Dedicated reservation is 2–4 weeks after contract, depending on region and capacity. We can often start the pilot on hosted while contracts progress.
05:38 Priya Natarajan: For the benchmark, what exact artifacts do you need from us?
05:42 Ethan Park: Ideally: (1) sanitized prompt set (~500–1k records) reflecting real distributions, (2) target JSON schema and function specs, (3) expected concurrency patterns (RPS, spikes), (4) an auth token or test API key if you want us to test against your staging endpoints for webhook flows.
05:58 Priya Natarajan: We'll prepare those. We'll also annotate prompts with desired ground-truth JSON where possible.
06:06 Sophie Chen: Great. We'll run an initial integration validation in week 1 (2-week pilot): get SDK wired, confirm function-calling and structured outputs; week 3–6 we'll run scale and cost validation and iterate on config (batching, quantization recommendations).
06:20 Daniel Reyes: Any blockers we should know about?
06:23 Sophie Chen: On Redwood side nothing major — we'll need your sanitized dataset and stakeholder availability. On legal — expect typical enterprise review, we'll send standard SOW and security docs.
06:33 Ethan Park: I'll own the benchmark runs and will attach a spreadsheet with assumptions: tokens per request, average completion length, concurrency, expected error rate, and machine configs.
06:43 Alex Martinez: Can you also include example SDK snippets in the POC pack? Our engineers prefer copy-paste.
06:47 Sophie Chen: Absolutely — Node and Python snippets, and an example OpenAI-compatible curl call. We'll also include the function-calling example and how to enforce JSON schema.
06:55 Priya Natarajan: One minor thing — do you support in-band tool calls to internal systems vs external webhooks? We sometimes prefer in-process mapping.
07:02 Ethan Park: You can choose function-calls to trigger webhooks or call a local adapter in your stack. We'll show both patterns.
07:10 Daniel Reyes: Cool. Let's recap action items.
07:13 Sophie Chen: Recap: Redwood send security pack + SDK examples (Sophie), Redwood run benchmark and share spreadsheet (Ethan), Nimbus share sanitized prompts and schema (Priya), Nimbus confirm pilot stakeholders (Daniel). We'll target the kickoff 2025-04-14 and bench results by 2025-04-09.
07:32 Alex Martinez: That works for me. Thanks everyone.
07:35 Sophie Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up with calendar invites and the docs.
07:39 Fireflies Recorder: Transcription ended.

Notes: occasional transcription artifacts observed (some product names slightly mis-heard), speakers sometimes overlap. Links shared in chat: /docs/redwood-poc-checklist, /security/soc2-v2.pdf, spreadsheet: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/nimbus-2025
